items.title: After the Cancellation of 'Call Me, I'll Hide The Body,' What Comes Next?
items.excerpt: Nigerian author Jerry Adedayo Falade's crime novel secured six- and seven-figure deals before being withdrawn from submission over AI-authorship allegations; Falade insists he wrote it himself and suggests the cancellation reflects bias. The case is becoming the industry's test of whether AI-detection signals can be trusted to end a book deal.

items.title: 'It was inevitable': Agents react to major book deal that collapsed over suspected AI use
items.excerpt: A crime novel that sold for $2.4m in a 14-way US auction was pulled by its agent on 31 July over suspected AI-generated content, and literary agents tell The Bookseller they now have no reliable way to authenticate how a manuscript was made. Agents describe uncertainty and fear becoming the default posture on submission.

items.title: Agent pulls manuscript from sale, 'no longer able to authenticate' its development
items.excerpt: Books+Publishing's account of the withdrawn crime novel focuses on the agent's stated reason — being 'no longer able to authenticate' how the manuscript was developed. It frames provenance-of-drafting, not output quality, as the new gate on acquisitions.

items.title: Study Claims Viral Bestseller DAGGERMOUTH is AI-Generated
items.excerpt: Stony Brook University researchers, using the Pangram detector, report that the bestselling dystopian romance Daggermouth is roughly 60% AI-written. The finding pushes AI detection from a classroom tool into the commercial bestseller list and raises the question of what a publisher does with a probabilistic score.

items.title: AI May Be Making Publishing Easier, But It's Still Not Easy
items.excerpt: Reporting from the Media Transformation Summit on how AI is reshaping publishing workflows: production and packaging costs have collapsed, but deciding what to make and getting it in front of readers is unchanged. A useful corrective for teams assuming tooling speed equals editorial leverage.

items.title: Poetry Foundation Library Scraped, Used to Make AI-Generated Educational Content
items.excerpt: Poet Kyle Dargan found hundreds of copyrighted poems from the Poetry Foundation site republished without permission by Giggle Academy, a nonprofit ed-platform founded by crypto entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao, as AI-generated learning material. A concrete case of literary work being recycled into AI courseware.

items.title: Local secondhand booksellers suspect AI companies behind bulk orders
items.excerpt: Secondhand booksellers across Australia and New Zealand report unusual bulk orders from Canadian recycling firm Zoom Books and suspect the stock is feeding AI training pipelines; Zoom Books denies digitising books for generative AI. Shows the physical-book supply chain becoming a training-data acquisition channel.

items.title: Around the Book World: August 3, 2026 — agents rewrite their ethics code for the AI era
items.excerpt: The Association of American Literary Agents has revised its Canon of Ethics to cover 'emerging technologies,' effective 1 September 2026; the same roundup notes Korean 20- and 30-somethings reading more as a counterweight to heavy AI use, and Hachette's parent expecting $22m+ from the Anthropic settlement.

items.title: 'Clarity of Thought and Responsibility': Can the Pope Move the Needle on AI Regulation?
items.excerpt: Pope Leo XIV's 42,000-word encyclical on AI argues for ethical governance covering data ownership, worker protection and education, warning that 'a handful of actors' should not dictate the terms. Publishers are reading it as unusually specific moral cover for creator-side AI policy.

items.title: Guest Post — The Third Time is NOT the Charm: Who Will Own How AI Participates in Scholarship?
items.excerpt: Argues scholarly publishing has twice built foundational infrastructure only to let others capture the value layer on top, and that the AI participation layer is the third and possibly last chance. A standards-vs-cede-control framing for anyone shipping AI features on top of a content catalog.

items.title: Researchers attempt to prove that generative AI dilutes the market for books
items.excerpt: Jane Friedman walks through new research trying to demonstrate empirically — rather than rhetorically — that generative AI output dilutes the market for human-written books. The evidence question matters because 'market harm' is the hinge of nearly every AI copyright argument authors are making.

items.title: Legal Battle Over U.S. Copyright Chief Heats Up Again
items.excerpt: The fight over who runs the U.S. Copyright Office is back in court, and the outcome shapes how the office rules on AI training and AI-assisted authorship registration. Lower-priority for a craft-focused brief, but it is the policy substrate under every AI-and-books story this week.

items.title: Princeton University Press partners with Cashmere on AI licensing
items.excerpt: Princeton University Press has licensed selected academic content to AI content-management platform Cashmere for copyright-compliant, non-LLM AI platforms. NOTE: likely dedup drop — the same story ran as an 08-04 card via Publishers Weekly; included only as backfill depth.
